title.en: Mixtures: hands-on activities from the textbook

text.en: Salt vanishes in water, chalk does not, and oil floats on top. Chapter 5 lets you test these differences and separate mixtures yourself.

Activity 5.1 prepares three mixtures in beakers, such as salt in water, chalk powder in water and a third type, and passes a thin laser beam through each.
In the salt solution the beam is not visible, but in the chalk suspension and in the colloid the particles scatter the light so the path shows. That is the Tyndall effect.
Activity 5.2 plots a solubility curve, solubility in grams against temperature, for two solutes A and B in water.
Activity 5.3 prepares crystals, for example of copper sulfate or common salt, by cooling a saturated solution. Copper sulfate is toxic, so work under supervision.
Activity 5.5 does paper chromatography. Mark a spot of black sketch pen 2 cm from the bottom of the strip and dip the strip's end in water, and the colours of the ink separate.
Activity 5.6 pours mustard oil and water into a separating funnel. Two layers form and the oil, being lighter, floats on top and can be run off.
Activity 5.7 heats camphor mixed with sand under an inverted funnel with a cotton plug. Camphor sublimes and its vapour collects on the funnel as solid camphor while the sand stays behind.
Activity 5.8 builds a model centrifuge from a cardboard disc and thread to see that heavier particles move outward when spun. Activity 5.9 compares solutions, suspensions and colloids in a table.

problem.en: Which method separates mustard oil from water, and which separates camphor from sand?

text.en: Oil and water do not mix and form two layers, so use a separating funnel.
Camphor sublimes on heating but sand does not, so use sublimation.
Each method uses a different physical property.

prompt.en: Explain how the laser beam shows the difference between a solution and a suspension.

requiredIdeas.en: Beam scattered by particles in suspension and colloid

points.en: Solutions do not scatter a light beam; suspensions and colloids do.
Chromatography separates coloured substances in ink.
Immiscible liquids separate with a separating funnel.
A substance that sublimes can be separated from sand by heating.
